questions.q: What metric does real-time (online) inference infrastructure typically optimize for?
options: Total records scored per hour, regardless of any single response's delay
The size of the container image
p99 latency — how slow the slowest 1% of requests are
The number of GPU nodes in the cluster
questions.explain: Real-time inference serves a caller who is blocked waiting right now, so the metric that matters is p99 latency rather than aggregate throughput.

questions.q: Why is a Kubernetes Job (or CronJob), rather than a long-running Deployment, usually the right primitive for batch inference?
options: Jobs run on CPU-only nodes and cannot use GPUs at all
The batch workload starts, processes a known amount of work, and stops — it doesn't need anything running continuously
Deployments cannot mount persistent storage
Jobs automatically retrain the model after scoring finishes
questions.explain: Batch inference scores a known set of inputs on a schedule and then stops, which matches a Job/CronJob's run-to-completion model rather than a Deployment's always-running one.

questions.q: Why do Spot/preemptible GPU instances make more sense for nightly batch scoring than for a live, user-facing inference Deployment?
options: Spot GPUs are only available for CPU workloads
Batch jobs are not allowed to request GPU resources under any cloud provider's quota system
Spot instances always cost more than on-demand instances
An interruption during a batch job just means a retry from a checkpoint, while an interruption mid-request on the live path is a failed user-facing call
questions.explain: A batch job can tolerate preemption by retrying; a real-time request that's interrupted mid-flight becomes a failed response to a waiting user, so the cost of an interruption is very different.

questions.q: What does "dynamic (request) batching" do in a real-time serving path?
options: It permanently stores every request in a database for later batch reprocessing
It converts all real-time traffic into an overnight batch job
It groups several near-simultaneous requests into one GPU call for a few milliseconds, raising throughput without breaking the latency budget
It disables autoscaling so the pod count never changes
questions.explain: Dynamic batching holds incoming requests for a short window, processes them together in one GPU call, and returns each caller its own result — getting some of batch inference's throughput benefit inside a real-time latency budget.

questions.q: Why can't a real-time inference Deployment scale from zero replicas the way a batch Job can start from nothing?
options: A cold GPU process can take minutes to load model weights into VRAM and warm up, which a synchronous caller waiting on a response can't tolerate
Kubernetes Deployments are physically incapable of running on GPU nodes
Real-time traffic never varies, so scaling is never needed
readinessProbe fields are only valid on Jobs, not Deployments
questions.explain: Because loading weights and warming CUDA kernels can take minutes, real-time serving typically keeps a baseline of warm replicas rather than scaling reactively from zero per request.
